questions.q: Why is calling only torch.manual_seed(42) often insufficient for full reproducibility?
options: torch.manual_seed only works on CPU tensors
Python's random module and NumPy maintain their own independent random states that are not seeded by torch.manual_seed
torch.manual_seed must be called once per epoch, not once at the start
torch.manual_seed is deprecated and no longer functions
questions.explain: random, NumPy, and PyTorch each have separate RNG state. If your data pipeline uses random or numpy for shuffling or augmentation, those need to be seeded independently of torch.manual_seed.

questions.q: What does torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) do, and what does it cost?
options: It speeds up training by skipping unnecessary gradient computations, at no cost
It forces PyTorch to only use operations with deterministic implementations (erroring on ones without), at the cost of potentially slower execution than non-deterministic alternatives
It disables all randomness in the dataset, with no performance impact
It only affects model saving and loading, not training speed
questions.explain: Some GPU operations have faster implementations that sacrifice determinism. Forcing deterministic algorithms avoids that run-to-run variation but can mean falling back to slower, deterministic kernels.

questions.q: A DataLoader uses num_workers=4 and a dataset whose __getitem__ applies random augmentation. The main process is seeded correctly, but results still aren't reproducible. What is the likely cause?
options: num_workers must always be 0 for any reproducibility
Each worker process has its own random state that is not automatically seeded by the main process's seed; a worker_init_fn is needed
DataLoader does not support reproducibility under any configuration
The dataset's __getitem__ method cannot use randomness at all
questions.explain: Worker processes spawned by DataLoader get independent random states. Without a worker_init_fn to seed each one explicitly, their augmentation randomness varies between runs even if the main process is seeded.

questions.q: What does 'reproducible' realistically mean in practice, according to this lesson?
options: Bit-for-bit identical results are guaranteed across any GPU model or CUDA version
The same seeded run on the same machine with the same software versions produces the same result every time — not a universal guarantee across different hardware
Reproducibility is impossible to achieve in deep learning
Reproducibility only applies to CPU-only training
questions.explain: Exact bit-for-bit reproducibility is not guaranteed across different GPU models, CUDA versions, or PyTorch versions, since hardware can implement operations slightly differently. On the same machine and software stack, though, a seeded run reliably reproduces.

questions.q: Besides torch.manual_seed and torch.cuda.manual_seed_all, which cuDNN-related settings are commonly used together to reduce GPU-side run-to-run variation?
options: torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True and torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = False and torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True
torch.cuda.empty_cache() called every step
torch.set_grad_enabled(False) for the entire training loop
questions.explain: Setting cudnn.deterministic to True and cudnn.benchmark to False, alongside torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True), reduces the chance that cuDNN picks a faster but non-deterministic algorithm for an operation.
